report.title: Leaked IAM access key abuse: from repository leak to crypto-mining and S3 theft
report.summary: A CI service IAM access key committed to a public GitHub repo in a .env file was validated by an automated actor within 11 minutes. The actor enumerated the account, created a backdoor user with admin rights, disabled CloudTrail logging, launched GPU instances for cryptomining, and bulk-downloaded S3 objects. All subsequent activity pivoted on the newly created backup-svc user or reactivated disabled keys in a second account.
threat_actors: automated actor (validated via Tor exit node)
targets: CI service accounts, AWS accounts, S3 buckets, EC2 capacity

behaviors.description: Actor validated the leaked IAM access key by calling STS and IAM enumeration APIs from a Tor exit node.
behaviors.evidence: The first calls came from a Tor exit node (185.220.101.34) with the user agent aws-cli/1.33.12 Python/3.11.2 Linux/6.1.0-kali and were made by the leaked identity arn:aws:iam::123456789012:user/ci-deployer: sts:GetCallerIdentity, iam:ListUsers, iam:ListAttachedUserPolicies, iam:GetAccountAuthorizationDetails, s3:ListBuckets, ec2:DescribeInstances (every region).

behaviors.description: Actor created a new IAM user and attached AdministratorAccess policy to establish a backdoor account.
behaviors.evidence: The actor created a new user and gave it full administrative rights: iam:CreateUser userName=backup-svc, iam:CreateAccessKey userName=backup-svc, iam:AttachUserPolicy userName=backup-svc policyArn=arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AdministratorAccess, iam:CreateLoginProfile userName=backup-svc (console password set).

behaviors.description: Actor disabled CloudTrail logging and deleted the organization trail in us-east-1 to reduce visibility.
behaviors.evidence: In us-east-1 the actor stopped and later deleted the organisation trail: cloudtrail:StopLogging name=org-trail, cloudtrail:DeleteTrail name=org-trail.

behaviors.description: Actor disabled GuardDuty detector in us-east-1 to suppress security alerts.
behaviors.evidence: It also called guardduty:DeleteDetector in the same region. Both calls were made by backup-svc from the Tor exit node.

behaviors.description: Actor launched GPU-accelerated EC2 instances in unused regions using the compromised key, each with user data installing XMRig.

observables.note: Cryptomining instance launch in second region

behaviors.evidence: Within an hour the actor launched sixteen p4d.24xlarge instances in ap-south-1 and sa-east-1, regions the organisation had never used, each with user data that installed XMRig: ec2:RunInstances instanceType=p4d.24xlarge count=8 (ap-south-1), ec2:RunInstances instanceType=p4d.24xlarge count=8 (sa-east-1).

behaviors.description: Actor listed and downloaded objects from the customer-data bucket using S3 ListObjectsV2 and GetObject calls, exfiltrating 23 GB over 40 minutes from a Tor exit node.
behaviors.evidence: The actor listed and downloaded objects from the bucket acme-customer-exports using s3:ListObjectsV2 followed by thousands of s3:GetObject calls over 40 minutes, 23 GB in total, all from the Tor exit node.

behaviors.description: Actor attempted to grant public read access to the S3 bucket by modifying its bucket policy, which was blocked by SCP.
behaviors.evidence: The actor also called s3:PutBucketPolicy on the bucket to grant Principal: "*" read access, which was caught by the organisation's SCP and returned AccessDenied.

behaviors.description: Actor reactivated a disabled IAM access key in a second victim account and attached AdministratorAccess via role assumption.
behaviors.evidence: In a second victim account the actor instead called iam:UpdateAccessKey to reactivate a disabled key of an existing user and iam:AttachRolePolicy to add AdministratorAccess to a role it could assume.

candidates.title: IAM CreateUser With AdministratorAccess Policy Attachment
candidates.rationale: Creating a new IAM user and immediately attaching the AWS-managed AdministratorAccess policy is a high-fidelity indicator of backdoor account creation. The rule keys on the specific API pair (CreateUser + AttachUserPolicy with AdministratorAccess) by the same identity within a short window, which is rare in legitimate automation.
candidates.false_positive_risks: Legitimate admin onboarding scripts that create users and attach admin policies. Mitigated by requiring the AWS-managed policy ARN (arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AdministratorAccess) and alerting on first-time user names not matching corporate naming patterns.

candidates.title: CloudTrail StopLogging And DeleteTrail By Non-Admin Identity
candidates.rationale: Stopping and deleting the organization-wide CloudTrail trail is a definitive defense-evasion action. The rule triggers on StopLogging or DeleteTrail where the calling identity is not a known break-glass/admin role (exclude known admin ARNs) and the trail name matches the org trail (e.g., 'org-trail').
candidates.false_positive_risks: Planned trail migration or region decommission by cloud ops team. Mitigated by maintaining an allow-list of authorized admin ARNs for trail management and requiring the trail name to match the known organization trail.

candidates.title: EC2 RunInstances p4d.24xlarge In Unused Regions With SSH Open To World
candidates.rationale: Launching GPU-accelerated p4d.24xlarge instances in regions the organization has never used (ap-south-1, sa-east-1), combined with a security group ingress rule opening port 22 to 0.0.0.0/0, is a strong cryptomining indicator. The rule correlates RunInstances with instanceType=p4d.24xlarge and AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress for port 22 from the same identity.
candidates.false_positive_risks: Legitimate GPU workload burst in new regions (e.g., ML training). Mitigated by maintaining a baseline of approved regions and instance types; alert on first occurrence in a new region with world-open SSH.

candidates.title: S3 Bulk GetObject From Tor Exit Node
candidates.rationale: Thousands of s3:GetObject calls against a single bucket (acme-customer-exports) from a Tor exit node within a short period signals data exfiltration. The rule keys on GetObject event count per identity per bucket per 10-minute window exceeding a threshold (e.g., >100) combined with sourceIPAddress matching known Tor exit lists or userAgent containing 'aws-cli' with Linux/Kali indicators.
candidates.false_positive_risks: Automated backup/restore scripts or data processing pipelines from EC2 instances. Mitigated by requiring the source IP to be external (not VPC CIDR) and/or userAgent indicating CLI from non-corporate OS (Kali, Tor Browser), plus volume threshold.

candidates.title: GuardDuty DeleteDetector By Non-Admin Identity
candidates.rationale: Deleting the GuardDuty detector disables threat detection. This is rare in normal operations. The rule triggers on DeleteDetector where the caller is not a known security-admin role and correlates with the same identity performing StopLogging (D2) for compound alerting.
candidates.false_positive_risks: Security team rotating detectors or switching to a different detector ID. Mitigated by allow-listing authorized security admin ARNs and requiring the detectorId to match the production detector.

skipped: B1: Enumeration APIs (STS, IAM, S3, EC2) are noisy and often legitimate; hard to distinguish from normal CI/CD or admin activity without multi-event correlation.
B7: PutBucketPolicy attempt was blocked by SCP (AccessDenied); failed attempts are lower priority than successful defense evasion.
B8: Reactivating a disabled key in a second account mirrors B2 pattern; covered by D1 logic extended to UpdateAccessKey + AttachUserPolicy.
plan.notes: All candidates use AWS CloudTrail logsource. Rules pair the API eventName with request parameters and identity context (userIdentity.arn, sourceIPAddress, userAgent) to keep specificity. Tor exit node IPs and unusual userAgents (Kali, aws-cli) are used as compounding factors where available. Baseline allow-lists for admin ARNs, approved regions, and instance types are assumed maintained by the SOC.

title: CloudTrail Trail Management by Non-Administrative Identity
id: 4719cfae-0b25-4cf3-9c21-78b18de6a547
status: experimental
description: Detects attempts to stop or delete the organization-wide CloudTrail trail by non-administrative identities, indicating
  potential defense evasion via disabling audit logs.
author: RuleSmith (Nemotron via Nebius Token Factory)
date: '2026-10-18'
tags:

logsource:
  category: network_connection
  product: aws

detection:
  selection_actions:

rules.author_notes: Focused on detecting disruption of organizational audit capabilities by unauthorized principals. The rule excludes known administrative ARNs while requiring actions on the specific org-trail to minimize false positives from general trail management activities.
rules.redteam_analysis: Positive variants P4-P9 cover realistic evasion surfaces: case variations on eventName (stoplogging, STOPLOGGING, deletetrail) and requestParameters.name (ORG-TRAIL, Org-Trail), diverse non-admin ARN patterns (cross-account assumed roles, service-linked roles, SAML federated sessions, EC2 instance profiles, Lambda execution roles, third-party vendor roles) that all lack the excluded admin/break-glass ARN substrings. Negative variants N1-N4 prove specificity: N1 and N2 hit the exclusion ARNs (role/Admin, assumed-role/BreakGlass) and must not alert; N3 uses a read-only eventName (DescribeTrails) outside the selection_actions; N4 targets a different trail name (dev-trail) failing selection_target_trail. These require separate detections.

rules.redteam_analysis: The six positive variants demonstrate realistic evasions that a well-written rule should still catch: they all produce an AttachUserPolicy event with the exact AdministratorAccess policyArn, but vary userAgent (boto3, terraform, console, aws-sdk-go, custom script) and/or username (lacking '-admin' suffix) so the filter_admin_onboarding (requiring both aws-cli/ and '-admin') does not exclude them. The fourth variant shows that using aws-cli but with a non-admin username also evades the filter. The three negative variants confirm specificity: two satisfy both filter conditions (aws-cli/ + '-admin') and one uses a different policyArn. The out_of_scope items highlight fundamental gaps: (O1) custom policies with equivalent permissions are invisible to a rule keyed on a single ARN; (O2) PutUserPolicy achieves the same privilege escalation via a different API call; (O3) credential theft and role assumption bypass user-policy attachment entirely. These are not failures of the logsource but of the rule's narrow scope; they are documented for the analyst to consider broader detections.

title: High Volume S3 GetObject From Suspicious Source
id: 013f712e-6c2c-48ba-b1ca-97e92899a39b
status: experimental
description: 'Detects excessive S3 GetObject requests (>100 per 10 min) from a Tor exit node or non-corporate CLI (e.g., aws-cli
